flavorUSM.6.d: Chen Dongyang, courtesy name Manyue, was the leading voice of citizen republicanism in the Western Qin Revolution and one of the founders of its short-lived republic. Driven out of the state he had helped create, he joined the southern progressives and, as chief minister of Southern Ming, became the leader of its modernising reforms.\n\nNow he is dead. The southern republicans who followed him have lost their mainstay, and the cabinet and Six Ministries must parcel out the duties he left behind. The provincial delegates are still arguing over the future of reform in the Assembly of Rites, but Hangzhou is already courting the leaderless officials.
ce_usm_cw_japanese_interest_reason: The Toyotomi shogunate once ended the Warring States with the backing of the Ming Prince of Wu, and in the struggle for Korea joined him to defeat a Korea backed by the Ming court at Yanjing and the old Qi fief. From then on, the Zheng foothold in Kyushu became one link in Wu's maritime empire.\n\nNow the South is at war with itself, and envoys keep crossing the sea, asking Japan for ships and supplies. The chance to recover the Wu-held lands of Kyushu is right in front of us.
usm_civilwar.1.d: In the great hall at Jinling, no one is left who can stand up to the Zheng sovereign of Wu face to face. By the measure of China's thousands of years of history, a change of dynasty was only a matter of time. Yet those who cling to the old and those who chase the new alike believed our age had risen above history. Dreams seldom survive contact with reality.\n\nThe Zheng have now called for a new dynasty and demanded that the provinces and overseas states adopt the Wu calendar. Hangzhou holds the army and the purse, but the Zhu line, centuries old, still has its loyal followers. The quarrel that the Assembly of Rites and the cabinet could never settle has at last reached the provinces. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must give its answer.
usm_civilwar.1.1: Wu bandits! Curs! Traitors! Villains! Usurpers!
usm_civilwar.1.2: The sage does not stand beneath a collapsing wall. How can good men dwell in a traitor's land?
usm_civilwar.1.3: How does the new regime's black hat feel?
usm_civilwar.2.d: Manifestos against the usurpation have spread to every province. Wu is mustering the central army to make the provinces accept Zheng rule; the Ming loyalist provinces are rallying their garrisons and scraping together men and grain for a common fight. The Southern and Western Administrations, who once stood shoulder to shoulder against the North, have come to blows after all.\n\nFrom the Far East Continent to distant England, the powers have sent envoys to ask what is happening. They will watch the East burst into flames once more after only a brief peace.
usm_civilwar.2.1: Send word to every camp: muster the men and the money at once!
usm_civilwar.2.2: By Heaven's mandate, end the nation's calamity! Slay the usurpers, restore the true calendar!
usm_civilwar.2.3: Better to die for the broad light of our state than live serving partitionist kings! Long live the citizens! Long live the republic!
usm_civilwar.2.4: When a minister coerces his lord from below, the Warring States age begins anew. Even Zheng pride has withered at last.
usm_civilwar.3.d:
Rather than let the conflict explode, the South's statesmen used a string of decisive measures to put off the empire's collapse. Even through an upheaval as great as the passing of Ming to Wu, the provinces and overseas states that stayed loyal never took up arms, and swallowed the Wu account of a Ming court rotten to the core; a few others simply left the old hierarchy.

In a sense, the dynasty of sun and moon may long since have become a rotten trunk that no one would follow into the grave.

Yet this survivor, which crawled out of long centuries of military fiefdoms, has also lost a great deal. Opponents, regional prejudice between the peoples of the old fiefs, and new radical societies still move in the shadows of the new age, laying a thick fog over the country's road ahead.
usm_civilwar.3.1: I too once wished to live in the age of Ming.
usm_civilwar.10.t: Victory in the Second Jingnan War
usm_civilwar.10.d: The civil war unleashed by the treacherous Zheng has ended at last in victory for us, the upholders of the rightful way. It was not an age to be proud of. Loyal servants slaughtered loyal servants, and republicans denounced republicans.\n\nOnly now that the war is won do the real difficulties come to the table. The Zhu house wants its throne back, the victorious provincial leaders will not give up their military and civil power, and the republicans want the citizens who fought side by side brought into a new deliberative government. Who, then, is to rule from Nanjing?
usm_civilwar.10.1: Set chaos right and renew sun and moon under a new sky!
usm_civilwar.10.2: Wu's crime lies in disorderly governance, not central authority itself.
usm_civilwar.10.3: We couldn't win it in 1812. We'll try again today!
usm_civilwar.12.d: [SCOPE.sCountry('usm_mister_rebel').GetName] fought beside the coalition. No sooner was the Second Jingnan War over than they sent us a declaration of independence: they refuse to swear allegiance to the new central government at Nanjing that we represent, and mean to run their own army, finances and diplomacy.
usm_civilwar.13.d: [SCOPE.sCountry('usm_mister_rebel').GetName] has sent envoys to Nanjing to swear allegiance to the new central government. Having weighed strength and popular standing, they have traded the comradeship of the war for the bond between sovereign and subject; local civil and military affairs will now run under the terms newly agreed.
usm_civilwar.23.d: The Zheng and the rulers of Japan are old acquaintances. Truth be told, they have long been the masters of China in all but name; by the precedents of Chinese history, a master of the realm taking one step further would be nothing new, and if anything the Zheng have waited a long time.\n\nNow Wu and the provinces against it have both sent men across the sea to ask Japan for troops, and both offer the same price: the return of the Zheng-held parts of Kyushu after the war. Such a chance comes once in a hundred years.
usm_civilwar.23.1: We need leaders loyal to Shenzhou.
usm_civilwar.23.2: Support those who stand against Wu!
usm_civilwar.23.3: Perhaps our era has not yet arrived...
